71.outcome: Generate the same contained lake from either side of a chunk border, and explain why it cannot drain on activation.
71.why: A beautiful bowl drawn on top of water is not a contained lake. The actual occupied cells must hold the liquid, and generation must agree when neighbouring chunks are requested in different orders.

sections.title: Start with the failure, not the noise function
sections.html:
Imagine a basin whose left wall is in chunk A and right wall is in chunk B. If A fills water before B supplies its wall, activation can spill the lake. Generating more noise does not fix this. We need a world-coordinate feature definition that both chunks can evaluate independently. The feature owns its bowl profile and fill level; chunks merely sample it.

Use a handcrafted cross-section first: solid walls, level water and air above. Run 600 ticks before adding procedural placement. If this tiny fixture leaks, debug occupancy, absorption or boundaries before blaming generation.

sections.title: Bound the neighbourhood that can affect a cell
sections.html:
The design caps a lake width at 96 cells. Represent a candidate by centre, half-width and rim altitude. A chunk only asks for candidate centres close enough to overlap it. This is a finite dependency, unlike asking whether an arbitrary distant outlet exists somewhere in an infinite valley.

For a teaching bowl, let depth decrease linearly toward the rim: depth = half_width - distance_from_centre. A cell below the resulting floor is stone, between floor and water level is water, and above is air. This deliberately angular bowl proves the spatial contract; a smooth profile can replace the depth calculation later without changing ownership.

sections.title: Resolve feature ordering explicitly
sections.html:
Apply base strata, candidate bowl carving and water placement in a fixed order. Two overlapping bowls need a tie-break, such as the lowest feature ID, rather than whichever chunk happens to load first. Caves must respect the sea/surface exclusion band. Otherwise a valid lake can be drained by a later cave pass.

Water over generated porous soil must begin with the approved saturation state. If fresh water immediately disappears through absorption, that is a generation-state mismatch, not an excuse to weaken the rest test. Keep containment geometry and moisture initialization in separate assertions.

sections.title: Integrate one pure sampling function
sections.html:
The function below receives a world coordinate and returns a material classification. It has no mutable RNG, no chunk cache and no dependence on camera position. Sampling the same coordinate twice therefore produces the same result. In the real generator combine it with bounded candidate lookup and the existing material table.

Save the example as indicated, then call the sampler through your chunk-generation loop. Generate the left and right chunks in opposite orders and compare their output hashes. Finally activate the whole bowl, because pure generation equality cannot prove the water simulation rests.

worked.label: Complete focused experiment — save as examples/lesson_071.rs, then run cargo run --example lesson_071 from game/.
explanation: y is world altitude here, increasing upward. This is not the early downward screen-row convention.
The rim at distance == half is stone even at the fill level, containing water in the teaching profile.
The Air result outside the feature means no lake override; in production preserve base terrain there rather than replacing it with air.
worked.expected: bowl centre, rim and open sky agree

exercises.title: Trace the cross-section
exercises.prompt: At x=64, centre=64, half=12 and level=10, classify altitudes -3, 0, 10 and 11.
exercises.hint: Calculate floor before choosing a material.
exercises.solution: The floor is -2. Altitude -3 is Stone; 0 and 10 are Water; 11 is Air. The lake does not decide which altitude is on the screen.
exercises.proof: Write four assertions with those outcomes.

exercises.title: Put the lake on a seam
exercises.prompt: Move the centre to a coordinate exactly divisible by 64. Generate neighbouring chunks in both orders.
exercises.hint: Feature data should be computed from world identity, not load order.
exercises.solution: A centre of 64 puts the feature across chunks 0 and 1. Both evaluate the same centre/profile. Generate A then B and B then A, concatenate by coordinate and compare equal arrays.
exercises.proof: The combined arrays and activation behavior agree.

exercises.title: Make a deliberately broken cave
exercises.prompt: Carve one air cell through a bowl wall below the water level. Explain the resulting rest-test failure.
exercises.hint: A lake is only contained by actual cells.
exercises.solution: Water exits through the hole under the existing movement rule. Restore the wall or constrain the cave feature. Changing the decorative shoreline cannot repair a missing solid.
exercises.proof: The broken fixture moves water; restoring the cell prevents that escape.

troubleshooting.cause: Bowl geometry or generated moisture is inconsistent with movement/absorption.
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect a tiny cross-section and saturation before widening the fixture.

troubleshooting.cause: Features were chosen by mutable RNG consumption or different local origins.
troubleshooting.fix: Select candidates in world coordinates with a deterministic tie-break.

troubleshooting.cause: Feature ordering has no exclusion constraint.
troubleshooting.fix: Check cave placement against the generated surface/sea and bounded feature geometry.

72.outcome: Move a labelled owned result from a worker to the main thread using a bounded channel.
72.why: Generation and disk work should not freeze drawing, but letting a worker mutate the live world makes ownership and timing harder. A message lets one owner finish work and transfer the result at a controlled point.

sections.title: Discover the ownership boundary
sections.html:
The main loop owns the live world. A worker owns a request while processing it, then owns the produced data. Sending a message transfers that data; receiving it gives the main loop the opportunity to install it. The worker does not need a permanent mutable reference to the whole world.

Start with one labelled result rather than a full threaded loader. If you cannot point to the owner before and after send, pause here and revisit moves. A String or Vec in a sent message moves; a small Copy identifier behaves differently.

sections.title: Bound the queue before making it fast
sections.html:
An unbounded channel can accumulate work faster than a slow disk or generator finishes it. A sync_channel with a finite capacity applies backpressure. Blocking send is acceptable inside a worker, but a full request queue must not block the rendering thread. For main-loop requests, use a nonblocking send policy or cap outstanding requests.

A capacity of two in the experiment is an instructional limit, not a tuned game value. Measure queue depth and memory in production. A camera flying across terrain should not enqueue every obsolete intermediate chunk forever.

sections.title: Reject stale results by identity
sections.html:
A result needs both its chunk coordinates and the world/request generation it belongs to. Imagine loading world A, requesting chunk (0,0), then switching to world B before the worker replies. Coordinates alone match, but installing A’s data into B corrupts the new world.

Compare a world epoch or request token when receiving. Discard or cache stale results according to an explicit policy. This is a correctness condition even with a perfectly reliable channel and no data races.

sections.title: Receive without freezing the frame
sections.html:
The complete example uses recv once because a terminal demo has nothing to draw while waiting. In the game use try_recv in a bounded drain loop, stopping after a message/time allowance. An empty queue is not an error requiring a panic. Disconnection means all relevant senders have gone away; decide how to surface worker failure.

Keep a JoinHandle and define shutdown: stop accepting work, drop request senders, let the worker exit or cancel cooperatively, then join. A thread does not automatically stop because the camera no longer needs its result.

worked.label: Complete focused experiment — save as examples/lesson_072.rs, then run cargo run --example lesson_072 from game/.
explanation: move transfers the sender into the worker closure; it does not borrow the main stack indefinitely.
The payload vector is moved through the message. No second mutable alias to those cells is created.
expect is used to make a tiny controlled experiment fail loudly; production handles disconnects through Result.

exercises.title: Reject the wrong world
exercises.prompt: Change live_epoch to 8. What should be installed?
exercises.hint: Do not change the reply to make the test pass.
exercises.solution: Nothing is installed because reply epoch 7 does not match live epoch 8. Add an explicit stale-result counter and assert it increments.
exercises.proof: No chunk data from the previous world enters the current map.

exercises.title: Protect the frame loop
exercises.prompt: Replace the terminal waiting receive with a game-loop-friendly receive strategy.
exercises.hint: An empty queue is normal between completed jobs.
exercises.solution: Use try_recv; handle Ok(reply), Empty by stopping this frame’s drain, and Disconnected by reporting worker status. Bound the number of replies installed per frame.
exercises.proof: An empty queue returns control immediately.

exercises.title: Explain backpressure
exercises.prompt: A worker sends three replies to capacity two without a receiver draining. Where does it wait?
exercises.hint: Count queued messages, not total sends.
exercises.solution: The first two replies fill the queue. A blocking third send waits until capacity is available or the receiver disconnects. Never perform that blocking path on the drawing thread.
exercises.proof: A small controlled test demonstrates blocking or uses try_send to observe Full.

troubleshooting.cause: Main loop called recv or blocking send.
troubleshooting.fix: Use nonblocking main-loop queue operations and bounded work.

troubleshooting.symptom: Old terrain appears after loading another world
troubleshooting.cause: Replies are checked only by chunk coordinates.
troubleshooting.fix: Include and compare a world/request epoch.

troubleshooting.cause: A sender remains alive or the worker has no shutdown condition.
troubleshooting.fix: Drop request senders deliberately and join workers once their loop can terminate.

73.outcome: Propagate a recoverable file error to a caller that prints a useful message and keeps running.
73.why: A missing save is an expected external condition. It should lead to a useful choice—new world, backup or another path—not a panic that throws away the current session.

sections.title: Begin with two possible outcomes
sections.html:
An integer-returning parser cannot say both “the value is zero” and “there was no valid value” using zero alone. Result keeps those outcomes separate. Its Ok variant contains the successful value; Err contains failure information. Which action follows belongs to the caller, not automatically to the low-level parser.

For a save header reader, success means validated metadata. Failure might mean the file cannot be read, the bytes are invalid or the version is unsupported. Preserve enough context to distinguish them. Do not turn every error into “save missing.”

sections.title: Follow the question mark through one function
sections.html:
The ? operator on a Result unwraps the success path for continued processing, or returns the error early through a compatible Result-returning function. It does not log, retry, choose a backup or repair data. Those decisions remain visible at the boundary where the operation is presented to the player.

First write the function using match on fs::read_to_string. Then replace the early-return pattern with ?. Compare the two versions. The shorter syntax is valuable only after the control flow is understood.

sections.title: Validate after reading
sections.html:
A successful read proves bytes were obtained, not that they form a valid world. Trim text in this teaching experiment, parse the number and map parser failure into an io::Error with InvalidData. A binary loader will later validate magic bytes, versions, lengths and material identifiers in the same logical order.

Keep this terminal experiment separate from real world saves. Its small text format is not the production format. We are learning failure flow before coupling it to chunks and background writers.

sections.title: Handle failure where context is available
sections.html:
The main function knows which path the user requested. It can print that path with the underlying error and leave the current world untouched. In production attach operation context, preserve the prior save and offer recovery. A low-level decoder should not reach into the UI to display a dialog.

Test both success and failure intentionally. A happy-path demonstration alone leaves the useful half of this lesson untested. Missing files, invalid text and permission failures may require different recovery messages even though all return Err.

worked.label: Complete focused experiment — save as examples/lesson_073.rs, then run cargo run --example lesson_073 from game/.
explanation: Run with no lesson-seed.txt first; failure is part of the exercise, not a broken installation.
Create the file containing 42 and run again to see the success branch.
A failed parse becomes InvalidData; a failed read keeps the filesystem error kind.

exercises.title: Make both branches real
exercises.prompt: Run once without the file, once with 42, and once with sand as its contents.
exercises.hint: The current working directory determines this teaching path.
exercises.solution: The first run returns an I/O error, the second returns Ok(42), and the third returns InvalidData. Only the caller prints the operation and path.
exercises.proof: Capture all three distinct outcomes.

exercises.title: Expand the control flow
exercises.prompt: Rewrite the first ? using match without changing behavior.
exercises.hint: Err must return from read_seed, not only print.
exercises.solution: Use let text = match fs::read_to_string(path) { Ok(text) => text, Err(error) => return Err(error) }; and leave parsing unchanged.
exercises.proof: The three fixtures produce equivalent success/error kinds.

exercises.title: Protect existing state
exercises.prompt: A world with seed 7 is live. Loading seed text fails. What must remain unchanged?
exercises.hint: Do not assign partially loaded data into the world.
exercises.solution: Retain seed 7 and all live world state. Construct and validate replacement state first; install it only after the load operation succeeds.
exercises.proof: A failed load fixture compares the live world hash before and after.

troubleshooting.cause: The enclosing function does not return a compatible Result.
troubleshooting.fix: Return the appropriate Result or handle the error locally with match.

troubleshooting.symptom: Missing and invalid files show the same message
troubleshooting.cause: Code discarded the original error context.
troubleshooting.fix: Keep the error kind and add the operation/path at the boundary.

troubleshooting.symptom: The file exists but the program cannot find it
troubleshooting.cause: The relative path is resolved against a different current directory.
troubleshooting.fix: Run from game/ or print the resolved path in the teaching experiment.

74.outcome: Encode a small explicit versioned header and reject truncated or unsupported input before using it.
74.why: An in-memory struct is a convenient Rust value, but its layout is not automatically a portable save protocol. We need byte meanings that future readers can understand even after the implementation changes.

sections.title: Decide what every byte means
sections.html:
Start with a tiny header rather than serializing the whole world. Our teaching header has four magic bytes, a little-endian format version and a seed. Magic distinguishes this file family; the version selects a decoding contract; the seed is data interpreted under that contract.

Write offsets on paper before code: bytes 0 through 3 are RSTY, 4 through 5 are version 1, and 6 through 13 are a u64 seed. That totals 14 bytes. Explicit byte order avoids depending on the host machine’s endianness.

sections.title: Validate shape before conversion
sections.html:
A loader first checks exact length in the small example, then magic, then version, and only then decodes payload fields. The order prevents out-of-bounds slicing and makes unsupported input fail before allocating world data. In a larger format validate each declared length against configured maximums before allocation.

Do not cast arbitrary bytes into Material or a Rust struct. Invalid enum discriminants and layout padding are not a public format. Encode material IDs deliberately and validate each accepted ID during decode.

sections.title: Keep versions about different promises
sections.html:
The header here carries only a format version. The full world also needs generator version, tick counters, changed regions and the other saved-state inventory. A format version answers how to read bytes. A generator version answers how to regenerate absent chunks. One number cannot safely stand for both.

Build the codec as a pure byte-to-value function returning Result. File reading belongs outside it. This lets tests supply truncated buffers directly without creating temporary files or opening the game.

sections.title: Prove equality and rejection
sections.html:
Round-trip equality means decoding our encoding returns the original metadata. It does not prove corrupt data is rejected; add negative cases for every validation boundary. Change one magic byte, try a future version and truncate at every byte position.

In the game, migrate this experiment into save/codec.rs and add payload-specific encoding. Keep a tiny known byte fixture in tests so an accidental endian or field-order change becomes obvious. Before a public format change, either retain the old reader or implement an explicit migration.

worked.label: Complete focused experiment — save as examples/lesson_074.rs, then run cargo run --example lesson_074 from game/.
explanation: All slices are reached only after the length check.
to_le_bytes/from_le_bytes define the file byte order independently of native layout.
This minimal format is a worked codec experiment; do not use it to replace the full world-state inventory.
worked.expected: header round-trip and truncation checks pass

exercises.title: Predict a field
exercises.prompt: What are the eight seed bytes for seed 42?
exercises.hint: The least-significant byte comes first in little-endian order.
exercises.solution: The seed bytes are 42,0,0,0,0,0,0,0. Magic and version precede them. Print the encoded vector and identify the offsets.
exercises.proof: Your predicted bytes match the produced buffer.

exercises.title: Reject future data
exercises.prompt: Change version bytes to 2 and 0.
exercises.hint: Do not silently interpret unknown versions as version 1.
exercises.solution: decode returns unsupported format version. Preserve the original buffer/file and choose a supported reader or explicit migration rather than rewriting it during rejection.
exercises.proof: The error path leaves the input unchanged.

exercises.title: Add a bounded payload length
exercises.prompt: Describe where a chunk count should be checked before allocating its cells.
exercises.hint: Check both a format limit and arithmetic overflow.
exercises.solution: Decode the count, reject counts above the region limit, use checked multiplication for bytes required, and verify the buffer has that many bytes before allocation/copy.
exercises.proof: A huge count produces a small error without a huge allocation.

troubleshooting.symptom: Round-trip works only on one machine
troubleshooting.cause: The codec used native memory layout or byte order.
troubleshooting.fix: Encode each public field explicitly with a documented endian convention.

troubleshooting.cause: The decoder slices before validating length.
troubleshooting.fix: Check lengths before indexing every variable-length section.

troubleshooting.symptom: Unknown material becomes a strange cell
troubleshooting.cause: The reader accepts unchecked IDs.
troubleshooting.fix: Map explicit accepted byte values to Material and reject other values.

75.outcome: Compress a bounded payload, decode it exactly and reject expansion beyond the declared cell budget.
75.why: Uniform terrain often compresses well, but compression must not become an unbounded allocation path. A simple run-length experiment makes encoding, expansion and limits visible before choosing a production codec.

sections.title: Understand a run before choosing a library
sections.html:
Consider material IDs [0,0,0,2,2,1]. Run-length encoding records three zeros, two twos and one one. This is useful for uniform spans, while alternating values can expand. Therefore compression effectiveness is a property of data and codec, not a promise that every chunk becomes a few kilobytes.

Our teaching codec stores a one-byte count followed by a one-byte value. Runs are limited to 255 so a long uniform span becomes several runs. This is a small educational format, not an instruction to prefer it over LZ4 without measurement.

sections.title: Put bounds before allocation
sections.html:
The decoder receives a maximum output length. Before each extension it checks whether the next run fits. It also rejects odd byte counts and zero-length runs. These checks make malformed input a normal Result error instead of a large allocation or ambiguous stream.

For production the maximum follows from a validated region index, up to 32 by 32 chunks and the documented cell encoding. Do not trust a compressed payload’s self-reported uncompressed size as authority. The external format and configured limits supply that authority.

sections.title: Group chunks without confusing identifiers
sections.html:
A region contains sparse changed chunks, not necessarily all 1024 possible entries. Its index needs local chunk coordinates, payload offset/length and enough metadata to validate each entry. Reject duplicate coordinates, out-of-range slots and overlapping payload sections unless a sharing rule deliberately allows them.

Compression can apply per chunk or per whole region. Per-chunk compression supports selective loading; whole-region compression may improve ratio but amplifies reads and rewrites. Choose based on measured panning and autosave behavior, and record the choice before freezing the format.

sections.title: Test content, limits and cost separately
sections.html:
Round-trip testing proves fidelity. Corruption tests prove rejection. Size/time measurements characterize usefulness. None substitutes for the others. Run uniform stone, alternating cells and mixed temperature/moisture payloads; material IDs alone underestimate the real save’s entropy.

Before adopting a codec dependency, check its primary documentation for maximum-output controls and error behavior, pin its version and review its licence. The worked standard-library codec lets us learn the control flow without installing a package; it does not settle the production compression decision.

worked.label: Complete focused experiment — save as examples/lesson_075.rs, then run cargo run --example lesson_075 from game/.
explanation: Runs never exceed 255, so 4096 equal bytes become 17 runs, or 34 encoded bytes.
checked_add prevents arithmetic overflow before applying the configured bound.
Use the full encoded cell payload in real measurements, not only material IDs.

exercises.title: Find the bad workload
exercises.prompt: Encode 100 alternating zero/one bytes.
exercises.hint: Every run has length one.
exercises.solution: The encoded output has 200 bytes, twice the input. A production format can choose an uncompressed representation when compression expands the data, with an explicit mode flag.
exercises.proof: Measure and report the expansion rather than claiming universal savings.

exercises.title: Reject a decompression bomb
exercises.prompt: Decode [255,0,255,0] with max=256.
exercises.hint: The second run would exceed the limit.
exercises.solution: The first run yields 255 bytes. The second proposes 510, so the decoder returns output limit before resizing.
exercises.proof: The decoder returns Err and never produces a 510-byte result.

exercises.title: Index sparse chunks
exercises.prompt: A region has changed chunks at local coordinates (0,0) and (31,31). Must it store 1024 payloads?
exercises.hint: An index can describe only present entries.
exercises.solution: No. Encode two validated entries and their payloads; absent chunks regenerate from the world’s generator version. Duplicate or out-of-range coordinates must be rejected.
exercises.proof: A sparse region round-trip restores both coordinates and no invented payloads.

troubleshooting.cause: The scene has short runs or high entropy.
troubleshooting.fix: Measure actual cells and support a raw mode when useful.

troubleshooting.cause: The decoder trusts declared expansion.
troubleshooting.fix: Enforce a validated maximum before every output growth.

troubleshooting.symptom: One chunk edit rewrites a huge region
troubleshooting.cause: Storage granularity and compression granularity are coupled poorly.
troubleshooting.fix: Measure per-chunk indexed payloads versus whole-region compression and choose deliberately.

76.outcome: Capture one coherent world state while leaving the live particles and chunks unchanged.
76.why: An autosave during a blast should not freeze debris in midair by returning it to grid cells. Saving asks what the world was at one tick, not how to modify the world into a shape that is convenient to serialize.

sections.title: Define a snapshot boundary
sections.html:
Imagine grain A moving from chunk 0 to chunk 1. Copy chunk 0 before the move and chunk 1 after it: the snapshot contains A twice. Copy in the opposite order and A disappears. Each chunk may be individually valid while the assembled save is wrong.

Choose a completed simulation tick as the logical boundary. Capture all needed values from that boundary before the next mutation can invalidate the view. For a first correct version, pause mutation briefly while cloning state into an owned snapshot. Measure the copy cost before optimizing with immutable pages or copy-on-write.

sections.title: Inventory state by its ability to affect the future
sections.html:
Chunks alone do not define the next tick. Include seed, generator/format versions, step/calendar counters, surface metadata, weather deltas, cooldowns and falling groups. Particle position, velocity and material payload also matter if loading should continue the same blast.

The current spec’s reinsertion-before-save rule deliberately mutates the live world. Treat changing it to particle serialization as a proposal requiring the corresponding spec update, not a silent compatibility fix. A saved snapshot can be coherent under either explicitly approved policy, but the two have different gameplay outcomes.

sections.title: Transfer the copy, not the live borrow
sections.html:
A writer job should own its snapshot after capture. Then the game can continue while a single writer encodes and writes the captured generation. The writer must not borrow a mutable World that the next frame also wants to update. Ownership is the practical boundary between simulation and I/O.

Cloning a large world every five minutes is not automatically cheap enough. Clone the changed/relevant state rather than every regenerated chunk, bound concurrent snapshots, and coalesce obsolete autosaves if the writer cannot keep up. A slow disk must not produce an unlimited queue of entire worlds.

sections.title: Distinguish exact continuation from exact timing
sections.html:
The experiment clones grid and particles together. Moving the original afterwards cannot alter the captured values. In production save the agreed scheduler residual state if exact scheduling continuation is part of the contract; otherwise document resetting it. A restored world hash can match while wall-clock timing still restarts differently.

Test a mid-transfer chunk fixture and a mid-explosion fixture. Save, continue, restore into a separate world, and compare the complete state inventory. Only then compare subsequent updates under the same injected inputs and tick multipliers.

worked.label: Complete focused experiment — save as examples/lesson_076.rs, then run cargo run --example lesson_076 from game/.
explanation: The snapshot has independent owned vectors because Clone clones each Vec element.
Capture occurs before any next-tick mutation in this experiment. A background writer must receive the captured owned value.
Fixed-point particle coordinates keep this experiment tiny; production particles may use the agreed floating-point representation.
