exercises.title: Find a missing field
exercises.prompt: Remove particle velocity from serialization but keep its position. What diverges after load?
exercises.hint: Compare the next update, not only the screenshot at load.
exercises.solution: The loaded particle begins in the correct place but follows a different trajectory because its future displacement is missing. Save the full agreed particle state or explicitly change the continuation contract.
exercises.proof: A one-tick continuation test detects the omission.

exercises.title: Construct the double-count bug
exercises.prompt: Copy the source chunk before a crossing and the destination after it.
exercises.hint: Count the same material ID in both copies.
exercises.solution: Both copies contain the transferring grain. A tick-boundary snapshot must capture either the before pair or the after pair, never a mixture.
exercises.proof: A count assertion fails for the mixed snapshot.

exercises.title: Bound autosave memory
exercises.prompt: The disk takes longer than the autosave interval. How should pending snapshots behave?
exercises.hint: More background jobs do not make the disk faster.
exercises.solution: Keep one active write and a bounded pending/latest snapshot policy. Preserve an explicit manual-save request if required. Measure snapshot-copy peak memory as well as resident chunk cache memory.
exercises.proof: Stress the writer queue and confirm memory stays bounded.

troubleshooting.cause: Particles are reinserted into the live grid to simplify saving.
troubleshooting.fix: Choose and document a full-state particle snapshot policy or explicitly accept reinsertion behavior.

troubleshooting.cause: A future-affecting field or cross-chunk transfer was omitted.
troubleshooting.fix: Compare the complete saved-state inventory at one tick boundary.

troubleshooting.symptom: Memory spikes during slow disk writes
troubleshooting.cause: Multiple full snapshots are queued.
troubleshooting.fix: Bound active/pending snapshot ownership and coalesce obsolete autosaves.

77.outcome: Simulate crashes at save stages and always recover a complete old or complete new generation.
77.why: A single writer prevents competing writes, but a crash can stop it between any two operations. The loader needs a commit rule that identifies a complete world rather than picking whichever region files happen to be newest.

sections.title: Find the multi-file failure
sections.html:
Suppose the world has regions A and B plus an index. Replacing A successfully and crashing before B leaves new A with old B. Per-file rename did its job, but the world transaction failed. A single writer serializes the operations; it does not combine them into one indivisible operation.

Use immutable generation-specific files or directories. Write all new payloads under generation N+1 without overwriting the committed N. The new manifest names exactly which immutable files form the new world. Do not ask the loader to guess from timestamps.

sections.title: Commit only the reference to complete data
sections.html:
The logical protocol is prepare payloads, verify/sync required data, write a manifest referencing those payloads, then publish the commit reference. Before commitment, load generation N. After commitment, load N+1 only if its validated files are complete. Retain N until the new state is known recoverable.

This is a design protocol, not a claim that one std::fs call provides power-loss durability everywhere. File synchronization, directory metadata synchronization and platform rename behavior must be checked on supported filesystems. A crash-recovery simulation proves logical ordering; real fault testing validates the implementation.

sections.title: Validate the manifest as untrusted input
sections.html:
A manifest needs a generation ID, format/generator identity and bounded region entries with integrity metadata. Validate entry count and paths; entries must resolve inside the world’s own save directory. Reject missing, truncated or mismatched payloads. If the newest committed candidate is invalid, use the explicit previous committed generation policy.

Avoid inventing a sophisticated recovery scheme before this two-generation model works. Keep errors visible and preserve both candidates until recovery is understood. Automatic cleanup must never delete the sole coherent generation because the newest directory merely exists.

sections.title: Make failure injection a normal test input
sections.html:
The worked model separates payload-written from committed. It deliberately does not touch the filesystem, allowing every stopping stage to be tested instantly and deterministically. Extend it with checksums and two region IDs, then connect the same state machine to actual writer operations.

Inject failures after each region write, after manifest write and before/after commit publication. A successful normal save is only one path through this state machine. Record the selected generation and complete world hash after every recovery case.

worked.label: Complete focused experiment — save as examples/lesson_077.rs, then run cargo run --example lesson_077 from game/.
explanation: complete is the model’s validated-data set, not a directory-exists test.
The commit reference chooses one complete generation. An uncommitted new payload cannot accidentally become current.
This pure state-machine model is a logic test, not an implemented durable filesystem writer.
worked.expected: every interruption selects a complete generation

exercises.title: Interrupt the region writes
exercises.prompt: Add two separate payload-written flags and crash after the first.
exercises.hint: A generation is complete only if all referenced payloads validate.
exercises.solution: Keep committed=1 after only new A exists. Do not include generation 2 in complete until B and the new manifest are validated too.
exercises.proof: Recover returns generation 1 and its full original world hash.

exercises.title: Reject a corrupt commit target
exercises.prompt: The commit reference names generation 2, but one payload checksum fails.
exercises.hint: Directory existence is insufficient.
exercises.solution: Validation must reject generation 2. Under the approved recovery policy, select the retained previous committed generation 1 and report that recovery occurred.
exercises.proof: No mixture of region versions is loaded.

exercises.title: Explain a safe cleanup
exercises.prompt: When may old generation 1 be deleted?
exercises.hint: Think about crash windows and retained recovery policy.
exercises.solution: Only after generation 2 is durably committed and validated under the platform-specific writer protocol, and only if the retention policy still keeps the required recovery history.
exercises.proof: Fault-injection tests never leave zero coherent recoverable generations.

troubleshooting.symptom: Some chunks revert after a crash
troubleshooting.cause: The loader mixes independently renamed region files.
troubleshooting.fix: Use a committed manifest selecting an entire coherent generation.

troubleshooting.symptom: Newest directory is loaded although incomplete
troubleshooting.cause: Recency is used as a commit signal.
troubleshooting.fix: Separate generation creation from explicit commit publication.

troubleshooting.symptom: Recovery deletes the only good world
troubleshooting.cause: Cleanup runs before new generation validation/durability.
troubleshooting.fix: Retain the prior committed state until the new protocol is fully complete.

78.outcome: Load an old world using its original generator even when the current default generator changes.
78.why: An unchanged chunk is usually regenerated rather than stored. That saves disk space only if the game remembers which generation rules originally produced it. Otherwise the edge of explored terrain can become a permanent seam after an update.

sections.title: Separate bytes from terrain identity
sections.html:
A format version explains how saved bytes are decoded. A generator version explains how absent terrain is produced from seed and position. The same format can store worlds created by several generators; the same generator can survive a storage format upgrade. Conflating them forces unrelated changes together.

Draw a world with saved chunk A and absent chunk B. Upgrade the default hill formula, then regenerate B with the new formula. A remains old terrain while B changes. The save loaded without a parse error, yet the world continuity promise was broken.

sections.title: Dispatch from the world, not the application default
sections.html:
The world metadata owns generator_version. Opening the world selects its generator implementation, and all future unsaved chunks use that implementation. A new-world screen may default to the latest generator, but that default must not leak into an already loaded world.

Use a small version enum parsed from explicit IDs. Unsupported IDs return an error. Never map unknown IDs to latest; that replaces a helpful incompatibility message with silent geometry corruption.

sections.title: Freeze released generation contracts
sections.html:
A generator contract includes seed interpretation, noise algorithm/version, biome thresholds, feature order and material placement details. Changing an indirect dependency can alter output even if your own function name remains v1. Pin dependencies and keep small expected-coordinate fixtures that detect changes.

Before first release the project may intentionally invalidate temporary worlds, with a clear message. After release either retain old implementations or design a deliberate migration. A migration must decide what happens at the seam between edited saved chunks and newly generated data; it cannot simply erase the player’s edits.

sections.title: Test absence as well as saved data
sections.html:
Round-trip fixtures generally cover stored chunks. Add a fixture where one known chunk is deliberately absent, then load using the old generator and request it. Verify its terrain hash and shared border against the historical expectation. This tests the part of persistence that has no payload to decode.

The worked example uses tiny height functions so the difference is obvious. In the real world pass generator identity through worker requests too; an old-world background result must not be installed after switching to a new world.

worked.label: Complete focused experiment — save as examples/lesson_078.rs, then run cargo run --example lesson_078 from game/.
explanation: These simple periodic heights isolate version dispatch; they are not the production noise algorithm.
The world retains V1 even when the application default is V2.
unwrap is confined to the controlled known-ID demo; real file parsing propagates the unsupported-version error.
worked.expected: old world keeps its generator; new worlds may use v2

exercises.title: Find the hidden seam
exercises.prompt: A saved old chunk ends at height 20, while the adjacent regenerated chunk starts at 40. Which version should be checked?
exercises.hint: Successful byte decoding does not settle generation.
exercises.solution: Check the world-owned generator version used for the absent chunk. The format can be correct while generator selection is wrong.
exercises.proof: Requesting the absent chunk uses the historical function.

exercises.title: Reject rather than guess
exercises.prompt: Replace metadata with generator ID 99.
exercises.hint: Latest is a new-world preference, not an error recovery policy.
exercises.solution: Return unsupported generator and preserve the world untouched. Ask for a compatible reader or migration rather than regenerating with V2.
exercises.proof: No chunks are generated or saved after the rejection.

exercises.title: Protect a released version
exercises.prompt: A noise dependency update changes V1 output. What test should fail?
exercises.hint: Use a golden coordinate/output fixture, not only same-run equality.
exercises.solution: Keep known seed/coordinate outputs or hashes from the released generator. Their mismatch detects algorithm drift even if two fresh runs agree with each other.
exercises.proof: Historical fixtures remain unchanged across unrelated updates.

troubleshooting.cause: Default generator replaced the world-owned generator.
troubleshooting.fix: Dispatch from saved generator identity for every absent chunk.

troubleshooting.symptom: Determinism tests pass but historical terrain changed
troubleshooting.cause: Only fresh-run comparisons exist.
troubleshooting.fix: Retain released generator output fixtures.

troubleshooting.symptom: Unknown version opens with strange geometry
troubleshooting.cause: The loader silently maps unknown IDs to latest.
troubleshooting.fix: Reject unsupported versions before generation or mutation.

79.outcome: Evict a changed chunk only after the exact saved revision has been acknowledged, without blocking camera movement.
79.why: The early cache kept changed chunks forever because it could not safely discard them. With persistence available, eviction becomes a small protocol: dirty state, queued snapshot, acknowledged revision, then release of memory.

sections.title: Identify the stale-acknowledgement bug
sections.html:
A chunk is edited to revision 4 and queued for saving. Before the writer finishes, the player edits it again to revision 5. The writer reports revision 4 saved. If the cache merely sees “save finished” and drops the chunk, revision 5 is lost.

Attach a revision counter to the chunk and capture that revision with the queued payload. Acknowledgement clears dirty status only if the acknowledged revision equals the current live revision. A newer live revision still needs saving. Coordinate identity alone is not enough.

sections.title: Treat eviction as a state transition
sections.html:
An unchanged regenerable chunk may be dropped immediately. A changed chunk becomes an eviction candidate, is snapshotted/queued, and stays resident until safe persistence is confirmed. Active chunks are protected from eviction. If the cache is over budget while writes are pending, apply the documented queue/memory fallback rather than discarding edits.

Use a resident-memory cap and an explicit accounting of pending snapshots. Otherwise the cache can appear bounded while the writer queue holds many extra cloned chunks. LRU means least recently used among eligible candidates, not blindly the oldest map entry.

sections.title: Coordinate loading and cancellation
sections.html:
A camera can request a chunk and leave before the worker returns. Label each request with world epoch and chunk identity; install only results still belonging to the current world. Deduplicate outstanding requests so the same missing chunk does not spawn a new job every frame.

For changed chunks, load persisted data. For unchanged absent chunks, regenerate with the world’s generator version. Keep the per-cell active rectangle separate from resident status: loading a chunk does not mean simulating all of its cells.

sections.title: Measure the whole panning pipeline
sections.html:
A useful stress run pans for thirty minutes while making periodic edits. Record resident chunk bytes, pending writer bytes, queue lengths and foreground frame spikes. A cache-size printout alone cannot prove the total memory bound.

The focused experiment below models revision acknowledgement, the most important correctness edge before integrating disk operations. Combine it with the bounded channels and committed writer already built. A failed write must leave the chunk dirty and available for retry or explicit error handling.

worked.label: Complete focused experiment — save as examples/lesson_079.rs, then run cargo run --example lesson_079 from game/.
explanation: The written revision describes a captured payload, not necessarily the current chunk.
An active chunk remains protected even after its current revision is saved.
A production revision counter needs an overflow policy; this short fixture isolates normal acknowledgement ordering.

exercises.title: Replay the race
exercises.prompt: Queue revision 8, edit to 9, receive acknowledgement 8. Is eviction allowed?
exercises.hint: Compare acknowledged and live revisions.
exercises.solution: No. The acknowledgement proves only revision 8 is persisted. Keep revision 9 dirty, retain its data and arrange a new save job.
exercises.proof: may_evict stays false.

exercises.title: Account for hidden memory
exercises.prompt: Resident cache is 64 MB, but ten queued snapshots are 16 MB each. What is the actual problem?
exercises.hint: The cache counter excludes owned copies in the queue.
exercises.solution: At least 224 MB is owned by these two components before other memory. Bound snapshot queues and report their bytes; a 64 MB resident cap alone is not a total-memory guarantee.
exercises.proof: A stress trace includes both resident and queued memory.

exercises.title: Handle a failed write
exercises.prompt: The writer returns disk-full for the newest snapshot.
exercises.hint: A failed write is not a save acknowledgement.
exercises.solution: Keep the chunk dirty and resident or safely retained by the pending snapshot policy. Report the error and pause/retry according to the approved memory policy, never pretend eviction is safe.
exercises.proof: The edit remains recoverable after the simulated failure.

troubleshooting.cause: A stale write acknowledgement clears newer dirty state.
troubleshooting.fix: Compare snapshot revision with live revision before clearing or evicting.

troubleshooting.symptom: Memory grows although the cache cap holds
troubleshooting.cause: Background queues own additional snapshots or duplicate requests.
troubleshooting.fix: Bound and account for all queues, not only the resident map.

troubleshooting.cause: Disk encoding/write happens on the frame path.
troubleshooting.fix: Capture bounded work and hand it to the single writer without blocking main-loop queue operations.

80.outcome: Produce a reproducible M4 acceptance report for generation, rest, streaming, memory and exact reload.
80.why: Finishing the procedural world means its parts work together under repetition. A single pleasant pan or successful load cannot reveal every boundary, activation or persistence failure.

sections.title: Turn milestone words into fixtures
sections.html:
The M4 gate promises long seeded exploration, rest and memory tests, and exact save/load. Give each promise a named fixture with seed, generator version, starting camera, input sequence and measured duration. Use the same fixtures after future changes so “still works” means comparable evidence.

For the rest fixture, generate 1000 chunks across the v1 biomes, run 600 ticks and count moved cells under the documented tolerance. Keep temperature/moisture initialization compatible with the generator so normal startup does not create avoidable motion.

sections.title: Separate logical clocks from wall-clock measurements
sections.html:
Simulation fixtures should inject ticks, not sleep for ten seconds hoping the scheduler happened to run the right count. Performance tests measure real elapsed time in optimized builds; behavior tests control world state and update count. They answer different questions.

Record hardware model, build profile, active-cell count, display size and thread count with timings. A faster developer machine cannot certify the floor machine. Include combined frame work, not only mean cell-update duration.

sections.title: Use exact comparisons only where promised
sections.html:
A save round-trip compares the agreed complete state, including the chosen particle/group and scheduler policy. A compressed byte stream can differ while decoded world state is equal; comparing only file bytes is not the semantic test. Conversely, comparing only visible colours can miss temperatures and cooldowns that affect the next tick.

For long-pan memory, track high-water marks and queue bytes in addition to ending memory. A run may finish under the cap after a large transient spike. Capture the largest observed resident/pending state and foreground stall, with a reason for each exception.

sections.title: Write a report another person can reproduce
sections.html:
Use a small table with fixture, command, expected result, observed result, hardware and pass/fail. Attach logs and one short clip showing a cross-border edit followed by save/load. State unresolved visual approvals separately; M4 is not M5 art sign-off.

The worked command sequence below assumes the named fixtures you built in earlier lessons. Replace filter names with the actual test names once and record them; do not claim they exist merely because the example mentions them. A failed condition becomes concrete remaining work rather than a green checkbox.

worked.label: Follow this worked procedure inside the learner-created game package.
worked.code:
# Run from game/ after adding the named fixtures in earlier lessons.
cargo fmt --check
cargo check
cargo test --release rest_generated_world
cargo test --release save_round_trip
cargo test --release negative_chunk_boundaries
cargo test --release stale_save_ack
cargo run --release

# During the recorded manual run:
# 1. Use the documented fixed seed and generator version.
# 2. Pan across all v1 biomes and edit across a chunk boundary.
# 3. Save; reload; compare complete agreed state hashes.
# 4. Record resident AND queued memory throughout the stress run.
# 5. Preserve hardware, timings and observed failures in the M4 report.
explanation: Test filters select real test names; no tests is not a passing fixture. Check the runner reports the expected nonzero count.
Use --release for the measured stress run, while keeping behavior tests deterministic and headless.
The manual part records actual observations. Comments in a command block are not proof that those observations occurred.
worked.expected: A report with actual fixture counts, rest tolerance, exact state comparison, memory high-water marks and unresolved failures—not just successful command exit codes.

exercises.title: Catch a false green run
exercises.prompt: cargo test rest_generated_world reports zero tests. Did the rest gate pass?
exercises.hint: Read the test count as well as the exit code.
exercises.solution: No. The filter did not execute the intended fixture. Fix the name/module path and require a nonzero expected count before accepting the result.
exercises.proof: The report records the exact executed fixture count.

exercises.title: Choose the right hash
exercises.prompt: A screenshot matches after load, but the water temperature differs.
exercises.hint: Future state depends on more than current colour.
exercises.solution: The semantic world hash must include temperature and all agreed future-affecting fields. The round-trip fails even though the screenshot looks right.
exercises.proof: The comparison reports the differing field or complete-state mismatch.

exercises.title: Report a spike honestly
exercises.prompt: The cache ends at 60 MB but peaks at 400 MB during panning.
exercises.hint: A final sample is not a high-water measurement.
exercises.solution: Record the 400 MB peak and queue contribution. The bounded-memory gate fails or requires an explicitly approved higher bound; the final value cannot hide the spike.
exercises.proof: The report includes the maximum observed total, not just the ending cache.

troubleshooting.symptom: Rest gate passes on one seed only
troubleshooting.cause: The fixture does not cover the required generated sample.
troubleshooting.fix: Record and execute the full chunk/biome set.

troubleshooting.symptom: Reload looks right but later diverges
troubleshooting.cause: The state comparison omits future-affecting fields.
troubleshooting.fix: Hash and compare the complete agreed inventory and subsequent fixed-input steps.

troubleshooting.cause: Seed, hardware, profile or input path is missing.
troubleshooting.fix: Store the full fixture identity and commands with the observed output.

81.outcome: Display an art-pixel image with nearest filtering while preserving four physical pixels per simulation cell.
81.why: The first window drew four logical units per cell at low DPI. A Retina window can map those units to more physical pixels. The finished art style fixes the physical grain, so the renderer must explicitly connect simulation cells, art pixels and display pixels.

sections.title: Derive the three coordinate spaces
sections.html:
One cell occupies two art pixels across. One art pixel occupies two physical display pixels across. Therefore a cell is four physical pixels wide. These multipliers describe units, not zoom preferences. A larger framebuffer should show more cells rather than magnifying the same cell array.

macroquad screen_width and screen_height are DPI-adjusted drawing dimensions. Multiplying by screen_dpi_scale recovers the corresponding physical extent. Perform budget and integer-pixel calculations in physical units, then convert destination coordinates back into drawing units when calling the API.

sections.title: Render details at the art resolution
sections.html:
A one-art-pixel crest rim is half a simulation cell high. Rendering one colour pixel per cell cannot express it. Build an art image with two-by-two art pixels per cell, draw the flat material fill, then place the rim inside the occupied top surface. Upload that image to a texture.

Set nearest filtering explicitly. Linear filtering blends neighbouring colours during presentation, softening hard silhouette edges. Nearest presentation preserves the chosen art values; fractional destination alignment can still create uneven pixel widths, so align the physical viewport and round dimensions as the design specifies.

sections.title: Separate the experiment from the production viewport
sections.html:
The complete example draws a 160 by 90 art image at exactly two physical pixels per art pixel. It centres that small image in the window so the unit conversion is easy to inspect. It does not claim to fill the final game viewport.

In the production path choose an art target from the budget-capped physical view rectangle. Its width/height are half that rectangle. Keep the border panel outside the world. Rebuild images/textures when the required size changes, not each frame. Update pixel content through the existing texture rather than repeatedly allocating GPU resources.

sections.title: Verify output with measurement, not appearance alone
sections.html:
A crisp-looking image can still use the wrong physical scale. Test low-DPI and high-DPI windows, then inspect a known two-art-pixel cell footprint in a captured framebuffer or reliable pixel measurement. Also verify mouse conversion against the centred physical rectangle.

Record odd-size behavior and platform DPI reporting. A UI text scale may change independently, but that must not silently change the world’s cell footprint. The experiment uses a static image to isolate rendering; integrate simulation uploads only after this unit contract is verified.

worked.label: Complete focused experiment — save as examples/lesson_081.rs, then run cargo run --example lesson_081 from game/.
explanation: The sand patch is exactly two-by-two art pixels, representing one simulation cell.
Destination size is 320 by 180 physical pixels, divided by DPI for the drawing API.
This static teaching texture avoids per-frame allocation; the live renderer updates an existing texture/image.
worked.expected: A small crisp image centred in the window; the sand cell measures four-by-four physical pixels on supported DPI configurations.

exercises.title: Calculate a Retina size
exercises.prompt: DPI scale is 2. What logical drawing width presents one four-physical-pixel cell?
exercises.hint: Divide physical units by the drawing scale.
exercises.solution: Two logical drawing units correspond to four physical pixels at scale 2. An art pixel occupies one logical unit in this case.
exercises.proof: A captured known cell has a four-pixel physical footprint.

exercises.title: Break filtering deliberately
exercises.prompt: Switch Nearest to Linear and compare a magnified edge.
exercises.hint: Inspect blended colours around the silhouette.
exercises.solution: Linear presentation introduces interpolated colours at scaling boundaries. Restore Nearest, integer physical alignment and exact dimensions for the game look.
exercises.proof: The restored edge has no interpolated colour fringe.

exercises.title: Avoid resource churn
exercises.prompt: Why should Texture2D::from_image not run every frame for a stable-size target?
exercises.hint: Separate resource allocation from content update.
exercises.solution: Allocate once and update its contents as needed. Reallocate only when dimensions or graphics resources require it; repeated allocation creates avoidable CPU/GPU work.
exercises.proof: A frame profile shows no steady-state texture recreation.

troubleshooting.symptom: Cells become eight physical pixels on Retina
troubleshooting.cause: Logical units were mistaken for physical pixels.
troubleshooting.fix: Use screen_dpi_scale and convert the physical destination to drawing units.

troubleshooting.cause: Texture uses linear filtering or fractional presentation.
troubleshooting.fix: Use nearest filtering and align the physical rectangle.

troubleshooting.symptom: GPU work spikes during every redraw
troubleshooting.cause: Textures are recreated inside the loop.
troubleshooting.fix: Retain resources and update data, reallocating only on size/resource changes.

82.outcome: Build a deterministic row-by-row sky ramp and place hard-edged celestial shapes without changing terrain.
82.why: Atmosphere should come from colour, light discs and weather rather than noisy terrain detail. The sky is also an opportunity to separate view composition from world geometry so camera movement does not reshape the land.

sections.title: Make the gradient a calculation you can inspect
sections.html:
Choose two approved RGB anchors and a span in art rows. For a row inside the span compute its fractional distance, then interpolate each channel. Clamp above/below the ramp rather than extrapolating into unexpected colours. A three-key dusk ramp performs the same operation in two segments.

Use exact computed colours with no palette snapping or dithering. The examples’ named palette anchors come from the art spec; intermediate time-of-day keys still need approval. A smooth ramp does not require blur: every row can be a solid exact colour while geometry remains pixel-edged.

sections.title: Rasterize a disc without softened edges
sections.html:
A pixel belongs to a flat disc when its squared distance from the centre is no larger than the squared radius. This integer membership test draws hard boundaries. A halo ring is another flat disc behind it, not an opacity falloff. A crescent subtracts an offset disc from the lit disc within the approved construction.

Place these shapes in the view’s sky composition while allowing actual terrain to occlude them. Do not teleport the moon each time a ridge approaches it. The reference composition target describes a chosen camera view, not a rule overriding free-camera geometry.

sections.title: Decide where sky can exist
sections.html:
Air in a cave is not automatically open sky. Use the approved exposure/background treatment to keep the sky behind exterior air and the underground treatment behind sheltered cavities. This distinction must remain visible when the player excavates and builds.

Stars are sparse single art pixels in eligible night sky, with the explicitly allowed dusk-star exception. Do not fill every empty cell with stars. Sun/moon reflections, bloom, god rays and soft glow remain prohibited. Adding a weather cloud layer requires the separate approved treatment, not a new decorative terrain range.

sections.title: Connect time after the still frame works
sections.html:
First freeze world time and render the same frame repeatedly. Record camera, palette keys and visual time so comparisons are reproducible. Then interpolate approved sky keys using world_tick and position. Celestial paths/phases need explicit keys and occlusion tests at dawn, dusk and short/tall views.

The following terminal helper isolates ramp math and disc membership. Integrate it into your art image loop only after the endpoints and boundary pixels are correct. Floating point here is a colour interpolation tool, not a replacement for the integer world/calendar state.

worked.label: Complete focused experiment — save as examples/lesson_082.rs, then run cargo run --example lesson_082 from game/.
explanation: The span must be positive; treating it as configuration with a validated minimum is better than hiding divide-by-zero behavior.
The helper clamps beyond the horizon endpoint, so lower rows stay at that approved endpoint.
Disc coordinates/radius in the actual art target are small; choose arithmetic bounds appropriate to production coordinate ranges.
worked.expected: sky endpoints and hard disc boundary verified

exercises.title: Predict a middle row
exercises.prompt: Interpolate halfway between channel values 20 and 100.
exercises.hint: Halfway means t=0.5.
exercises.solution: The channel is 60. Calculate all three channels independently; do not snap the result to a fixed palette.
exercises.proof: An assertion for the midpoint matches the helper.

exercises.title: Occlude the moon
exercises.prompt: A ridge rises across the moon while panning. What should change?
exercises.hint: Separate world geometry from celestial composition.
exercises.solution: The ridge occludes the moon where appropriate. Keep the approved moon path; do not move the terrain or moon to protect a reference composition.
exercises.proof: A pan capture shows natural overlap without shape teleportation.

exercises.title: Choose the cave background
exercises.prompt: An empty underground room is drawn with the daylight sky. Which condition is missing?
exercises.hint: Air material alone does not prove sky access.
exercises.solution: The background renderer must distinguish sheltered cavities from exterior sky-visible air according to the approved treatment. An underground view should not reveal stars through rock.
exercises.proof: The same world geometry renders a separate interior background.

troubleshooting.cause: Computed colours were snapped to a fixed palette.
troubleshooting.fix: Use the per-row calculated colour without palette snapping.

troubleshooting.cause: Canvas/graphics circle antialiasing or filtering was used.
troubleshooting.fix: Rasterize membership at the art grid and present nearest.

troubleshooting.symptom: Night sky appears inside a cave
troubleshooting.cause: Background choice checks only Material::Air.
troubleshooting.fix: Use the exterior/sheltered background rule rather than treating all air alike.

83.outcome: Build an actual-scale material contact sheet where required states remain distinguishable in day and night scenes.
83.why: If those states look the same, the simulation can be internally correct while its cause-and-effect story is invisible.

sections.title: Treat colour as an interface to state
sections.html:
A material ID supplies a base colour, while moisture, temperature, burning progress and variants may select approved changes. Use one coherent lookup rather than sprinkling colour arithmetic through simulation rules. Rendering reads state; changing a pixel colour must not change whether the material is wet.

Begin with the 21 launch material anchors from the current design. Then identify required distinctions: water versus ice, oil versus water, stone versus basalt, wood versus rotten wood, metal versus rust and smoke versus steam. A proposed palette is not approved simply because a function can return it.

sections.title: Compare pairs at the size players see
sections.html:
Large swatches hide tiny-cell readability failures. Make two displays: enlarged labelled swatches for discussing colour choices, and four-physical-pixel cells in a realistic terrain context. Inspect them under day, dusk, night and rain conditions.

Do not use random per-cell speckle as a shortcut. The art direction calls for flat materials or coherent ramps/variants. A wet-to-dry soil patch should lighten in an organized way that reveals change, while neighbouring unchanged soil provides a control. Avoid decorative texture that masks the actual state signal.

sections.title: Separate state appearance from event evidence
sections.html:
A static rust-coloured patch shows one state, but the required reaction also needs a visible transition within its deadline. Capture before and after with identical camera and lighting. For fire/lava and flashes, propose explicit brightness/saturation exceptions and check them against the no-bloom/no-reflection rules.

The contact sheet is not a substitute for reaction clips. It is a diagnostic that can tell us whether the reaction would remain unreadable even if the physics completed instantly. Add labels outside the game frame rather than adding permanent debug text to the release HUD.

sections.title: Make approval and accessibility concrete
sections.html:
Ask reviewers to identify the material/state without looking at its label. Record confusion pairs and revise only those until the complete scene remains calm and legible. Also inspect a grayscale or reduced-colour view as a supplementary diagnostic; it does not prove accessibility but can reveal reliance on barely distinguishable hue.

The helper below demonstrates deterministic wetness interpolation from a base dry to base wet colour. It clamps moisture to the supported range. The exact RGB choices are teaching values; the final scene-dependent keys must be approved, and temperature indicators must not accidentally introduce forbidden glow.

worked.label: Complete focused experiment — save as examples/lesson_083.rs, then run cargo run --example lesson_083 from game/.
explanation: The simulation stores moisture; this function only selects a display colour from it.
Clamping prevents an invalid renderer input from extrapolating beyond the chosen wet endpoint.
Use the contact sheet to decide whether intermediate keys actually communicate change at gameplay scale.
worked.expected: Five progressively darker soil colours for increasing moisture, with dry/wet endpoints exactly as asserted.

exercises.title: Separate rendering from physics
exercises.prompt: Change the wet-soil colour to blue for a diagnostic. Should ignition behavior change?
exercises.hint: Follow which state the fire rule reads.
exercises.solution: No. Fire reads material/moisture/temperature state, not the renderer’s RGB result. If behaviour changes, a simulation rule is incorrectly coupled to appearance.
exercises.proof: The same physics fixture hash is produced with both display palettes.

exercises.title: Find a confusion pair
exercises.prompt: At native cell size water and ice become indistinguishable at night. What should be compared first?
exercises.hint: Keep camera and lighting fixed while changing one variable.
exercises.solution: Build labelled and unlabelled paired samples, compare approved colour/value variants, and retest the freeze transition in context. Do not add sparkles or bloom merely to force distinction.
exercises.proof: A reviewer identifies the pair and sees the transition without a label.

exercises.title: Record a state transition
exercises.prompt: Prepare proof that drying is visible rather than merely a counter changing.
exercises.hint: Use an unchanged control patch.
exercises.solution: Capture wet-to-dry soil under fixed lighting and alongside a constant-moisture control. Record the state values and the visible colour change within the specified world-time deadline.
exercises.proof: Both the counter and on-screen difference are documented.

troubleshooting.symptom: Every material looks like grey noise
troubleshooting.cause: Independent per-cell variation overwhelms identity.
troubleshooting.fix: Use coherent state-driven colours and remove speckle.

troubleshooting.cause: Swatch review ignored four-pixel gameplay cells.
troubleshooting.fix: Include native-scale, scene-context comparisons.

troubleshooting.cause: Lighting changes mask the material transition.
troubleshooting.fix: Test with fixed lighting first, then approve the state signal under time-of-day variation.

84.outcome: Render rain that respects shelter while changing graphics density leaves precipitation physics unchanged.
84.why: The weather simulation already applies rain at the surface.

sections.title: Draw the causal boundary first
sections.html:
Use a debug cross-section with a roof and an open hillside. Mark the exposed surface for each column. Rain simulation uses its approved surface rule, while visual streaks are clipped before they pass into sheltered space. The two systems share world meaning but do different work.

A renderer may draw 300 or 1400 streaks depending on graphics settings. The same tick/input sequence must still produce the same wetness and runoff. If lowering visual quality dries the hillside, the simulation is counting decorative particles as real rain.

sections.title: Freeze a deterministic visual frame
sections.html:
For visual comparisons use a separate deterministic decoration seed/time. Generate candidate streak positions, rasterize short diagonal lines in art pixels and clip them against the view and shelter. The static frame in this experiment needs no animation loop to prove the clipping condition.

Keep decoration randomness separate from physics randomness. Adding one extra streak should not consume a random number that changes the next fire or growth decision. Use named independent streams or coordinate hashes with distinct purpose tags.

sections.title: Choose layering without breaking pixel rules
sections.html:
The approved reference has far and near streak tones; near streaks are composited last. Opacity blending of hard art pixels is allowed by the rain recipe; spatial blur is not. Clouds, snow and fog treatments remain proposals until approved. Fog should affect visibility coherently without softening the actual geometry boundaries.

Rendered sea ripples also stay cosmetic in v1. They may colour occupied surface-water pixels but must not create water into air or carry sand unless a later mechanical erosion rule explicitly does so. Keep every weather visual’s read-only relationship to simulation state visible in the code.

sections.title: Test the shelter edge and quality switch
sections.html:
A single streak can cross several columns, so clipping only its starting point is insufficient. Test every rasterized art pixel against the surface/shelter at that column. At the roof edge, exposed pixels outside the roof can continue while protected pixels beneath it are omitted.

The helper below reports which pixels from a diagonal candidate survive a small shelter mask. Integrate it with your integer line rasterizer, not an antialiased graphics stroke. Then replay the same rain simulation with two decorative densities and compare world hashes.

worked.label: Complete focused experiment — save as examples/lesson_084.rs, then run cargo run --example lesson_084 from game/.
explanation: These rows increase downward in the art mask; derive them from world altitude with the approved conversion.
Each candidate pixel is checked, so a streak cannot pass through a roof just because its start was exposed.
The function returns visibility only. It never changes moisture or creates Material::Water.
worked.expected: The candidate pixel above open ground survives; pixels at or beneath the roof are rejected.

exercises.title: Lower the graphics quality
exercises.prompt: Replay a rain fixture with 100 and 1400 decorative streaks. Which state should match?
exercises.hint: Compare the complete simulated state, not the rendered frame.
exercises.solution: World material/moisture/temperature/counters match for identical simulation inputs. Only the image changes. Independent decoration RNG prevents physics-stream consumption differences.
exercises.proof: The world hashes match while image hashes differ.

exercises.title: Fix the start-only clip
exercises.prompt: A streak begins above a roof but ends beneath it.
exercises.hint: A valid starting pixel does not validate the full segment.
exercises.solution: Rasterize its path and check visibility at each art pixel, stopping/omitting pixels when they enter shelter according to the approved mask.
exercises.proof: No rain pixels appear below the roof in the fixture.

exercises.title: Keep waves cosmetic
exercises.prompt: A water ripple colours one air pixel above the true surface.
exercises.hint: The art spec forbids decorative water from changing the apparent collision boundary.
exercises.solution: Confine the ripple colour to occupied surface-water pixels. Mechanical water movement remains in the simulation, and v2 shoreline erosion is a separate rule.
exercises.proof: The visible occupied boundary agrees with the cell fixture.

troubleshooting.cause: Streaks are composited without a world shelter mask.
troubleshooting.fix: Clip each rasterized pixel against exposed surfaces including roofs.

troubleshooting.cause: Decorative drops mutate simulation or share a consumed RNG stream.
troubleshooting.fix: Make decoration read-only and use independent deterministic random inputs.

troubleshooting.cause: The renderer uses antialiased strokes or filtering.
troubleshooting.fix: Rasterize on the art grid and present with nearest filtering.

85.outcome: Route one click either to the material bar or to the world, and make the selected material visibly unambiguous.
85.why: A beautiful material bar is broken if clicking Wood also paints a wood block behind the button. Input ownership is a behavior problem before it is a styling problem.

sections.title: Start with one click and two possible consumers
sections.html:
The application receives mouse position and button state. UI hit testing should decide whether that event belongs to a bar/control before any world paint command is emitted. Treat input as a command-routing step; drawing a panel over the world does not automatically stop the underlying code from reacting.

Choose coordinate units explicitly. The material bar is laid out in drawing/UI coordinates, while world picking also needs the physical viewport origin, DPI conversion and cell scale. Convert at named boundaries instead of mixing raw mouse numbers with chunk positions.

sections.title: Make pages data-driven
sections.html:
There are more materials/tools than ten number slots. Represent pages as arrays of entries with label, swatch, key slot and action. Q/E changes page; number keys select within that page. A slot’s index is not automatically a Material ID because the Tools page holds commands instead.

Use an enum for an entry action such as SelectMaterial or SelectTool. Keep selected state in one place so a key press and a UI click use the same selection function. Greyed/unavailable tool feedback must explain the actual cooldown/state, not merely look disabled.

sections.title: Keep selection and hints readable
sections.html:
A muted UI still needs a clear selection boundary and readable text. Use the approved panel/text/selection palette and independent UI scaling. At native four-pixel cells, excessively tiny HUD text can undermine an otherwise calm frame. Test the actual display sizes instead of reviewing only a zoomed screenshot.

Show day, season, clock speed and physics-limited/slowed state consistently. The player should be able to tell when seasons are accelerated beyond physical updates. Hints may fade after use, but key labels and current selection should not become ambiguous when time changes.

sections.title: Separate the hit-test model from drawing
sections.html:
The worked terminal function checks a simple row of ten slots. It returns a slot or no slot using a half-open rectangle: left/top inclusive, right/bottom exclusive. That convention prevents a boundary pixel belonging to two adjacent controls.

In the real frame first compute ui_consumed. If true, dispatch the UI action and skip world painting for that event. Otherwise convert to a valid world position and paint. Test gaps, edges, clicks while dragging from the bar, and hidden-UI behavior deliberately; dragging capture policy should not be accidental.

worked.label: Complete focused experiment — save as examples/lesson_085.rs, then run cargo run --example lesson_085 from game/.
explanation: The rectangle is half-open so its far edge belongs to outside/gap handling.
The helper returns a slot index, not a material ID; page data maps that slot to an action.
Production layout may contain padding/gaps, which must be included in hit-testing instead of pretending the visual and hit rectangles match automatically.
worked.expected: UI click selects slot Some(1); world paint=false

exercises.title: Find the boundary
exercises.prompt: For left=100 and slot width=32, which slot owns x=132?
exercises.hint: Use a half-open first slot [100,132).
exercises.solution: Slot 1 owns x=132; slot 0 ends just before it. The boundary is not a double click target.
exercises.proof: Tests agree exactly at each adjacent-slot boundary.

exercises.title: Prevent paint-through
exercises.prompt: The UI reports a valid slot but world input still paints. Where is the ordering wrong?
exercises.hint: Drawing order does not control event consumption.
exercises.solution: Handle selection first and suppress the world command for that consumed event. Both mouse and keyboard selection should update one shared selected-action state.
exercises.proof: A click test changes selection and no world cells.

exercises.title: Test page semantics
exercises.prompt: On Tools page slot 0 means Fire starter. Should pressing 1 paint Material ID 0?
exercises.hint: The page defines the action, not the key digit.
exercises.solution: No. Resolve slot 0 through the active page’s entry action. A SelectTool action routes to tool use rather than painting an unrelated material.
exercises.proof: Number-key and click selection choose the same visible tool.

troubleshooting.symptom: Selecting a material paints behind the bar
troubleshooting.cause: World command is emitted before UI consumption.
troubleshooting.fix: Route input through UI first and skip painting for consumed events.

troubleshooting.symptom: Number keys disagree with selected page
troubleshooting.cause: Slot index is cast directly to Material ID.
troubleshooting.fix: Map the current page’s slot to a typed action.

troubleshooting.symptom: Bar looks clickable where nothing happens
troubleshooting.cause: Hit boxes and scaled visual layout differ.
troubleshooting.fix: Derive both drawing and hit rectangles from the same layout data.
